why.1: Section 5.1 lists numbered start permissives. These include slide valve ZT-105 at or below the 5% start-position limit before start. Section 5.2 gives step-by-step start steps. The 30 s PDT-102 bypass is tied to Run Time, which begins when the soft starter Run FB first goes true.
why.2: Section 12 defines a rolling 60-minute record of start attempts, including failed starts, with an inhibit when 4 attempts fall in the window. Records are retentive across power cycles and there is no operator override. The HMI shows starts used, a 'Start Available In: mm:ss' countdown and a 'Start Limit Active' alarm.
why.3: Section 4 states that no HMI function shall bypass any trip and that OFF never bypasses trip logic. Level 2 (150 ppm) and break-glass act through a hardwired fail-safe ESD circuit independent of the PLC, tested with the PLC in Program mode. Section 10.4 covers detector fault or analog Bad (high-priority alarm, EF-201 high speed, 'NO GAS DETECTION' alarm), and Section 13 covers signal failure.
why.4: Section 14 states C-101 remains stopped after power restore and latched trips are retained. Auto-restart is disabled by default and, if enabled, only under explicit conditions: was running in AUTO, no latched trips, permissives met, start limit allows, 60 s staggered delay. Trips require the condition to clear plus a manual HMI reset (Section 9). Test F40 verifies this.
why.5: Section 6.4 sets the priority order (forced unload over load inhibit over normal control), and Section 6.3 states inhibits override load demand while still allowing unloads. Section 7.1 inhibits loading at 95% FLA and forces unload at 98% for 3 s until current is below 95%, with 2% hysteresis. Caveat: forced unload starts at 98% rather than just above 95%, but the override logic is clearly defined and prevents fighting.
why.6: The Section 9 table covers many items with condition, setpoint, delay, bypass and action, and reset is given generically for trips. However, several alarms defined elsewhere are absent from the table, including NH3 Level 1 alarm, EF-201 Fail to Start, detector fault and No Gas Detection, Discharge Temp Load Limit, Slide Valve Failed to Unload on Stop, and HP cutout. Per-item reset methods for alarms are not given, and NH3/ESD rows only reference other sections. So not every alarm and trip is listed in a one-by-one checkable form.

why.1: Section 4.1 lists seven start permissives, including slide valve at minimum (≤10%), with the PLC unloading first if needed. Section 4.2 gives the start steps in order. The 30 s low-oil bypass timer starts at the moment the run command is issued, which is a defined event.
why.2: Section 4.3 defines a rolling 60-minute start counter that counts each issued run command and is retained through power cycles. A fifth start is blocked. The operator sees 'Start inhibit: max starts/hr' and the time left until the oldest start ages out.
why.3: The break-glass ESD is stated to be hardwired and independent of the PLC, and detector fault and out-of-range behavior is defined in 8.3. The 150 ppm shutdown is never explicitly stated to be non-overridable or non-bypassable from the HMI. The only related statement is the general 'all protective functions remain active' under Manual mode, with no prohibition on HMI bypass or forcing of the ammonia shutdown.
why.4: Section 9 states there is no auto-restart on power restoration and that start-count history is retained. Section 2 states all trips latch and need the condition cleared plus a manual HMI reset. Section 8.5 forbids auto-restart after ammonia or ESD events.
why.5: Section 6 inhibits load pulses at ≥95% FLA in both Auto and Manual, overriding capacity-control load requests. It forces unload pulses at ≥98% for 10 s until current drops below 95%, with a 92% hysteresis on clearing the inhibit. This defines how current limiting overrides suction-pressure loading so the two do not fight.
why.6: The Section 7 table covers the PDT-102, TT-103, PT-101 and II-104 conditions with values and delays. Action and reset are given only generically in notes and Section 2. The ammonia 25/150 ppm alarms, ESD, instrument-fault trips and the failed-to-start trip are not in the table, and some have no delay. The PDT-102 alarm behavior during the bypass window is contradictory ('may still annunciate' vs 'suppressed'). Not every alarm and trip can be checked one by one with tag, value, delay, action and reset.

why.1: Section 1.1 requires every step to have entry permissives, actions, completion criteria and a step timeout [TBC], and says a timeout raises an alarm and holds the sequence. Steps list concrete completion criteria such as PT-210 stable, 2 h turning gear run, PT-220 vacuum, 3600 rpm and the sync window. Steps also give specific failure actions: turning gear timer reset if M-15 stops, a trip if the turning gear is not disengaged, the sequence staying in hold on vibration alarm during a warm-up hold, and alarm with auto-sync disabled on sync timeout.
why.2: Step 8 and Section 2.6 say a HOLD or lower setpoint is inhibited inside 1600-1900 rpm. A hold request continues to 1900 rpm and holds above the band. A speed stall beyond the dwell time drives speed below 1600 rpm with an alarm, with an optional trip.
why.3: Section 2.9 has P-11 auto-starting (and recommends starting it on trip) as the MOP output decays. Section 2.4 provides P-12 auto-start on low pressure, on AC failure and on P-11 failure. The turning gear engages automatically at confirmed zero speed, with an alarm and manual barring if engagement fails.
why.4: Section 2.1 puts trips in a dedicated ETS or the governor protection function, with independent overspeed per API 670. The DCS gives alarms and interlocks only and is not the primary trip path. Monitor trips and manual trips are hardwired, pump auto-starts are hardwired, and Section 1.1 says overspeed does not depend on the DCS.
why.5: Section 2.1 says all trips latch, reset needs the cause cleared plus a deliberate operator reset, and first-out is time-stamped. Step 5 accepts the reset only if all trip conditions are healthy. A trip aborts the sequence (1.1 item 7), so a restart must go back through the Step 5 start permissives P1-P12.
why.6: Values not given in the input are marked [TBC] throughout. Section 3 flags the warm/hot start hold times, the 2oo2 vibration voting losing protection on a single probe failure, the tight 0.7/0.6 barg lube oil margin, the mechanical bolt tolerance, the unspecified thrust and overspeed voting, and the vibration tag list ambiguity.

why.1: Only a few steps have explicit completion criteria. Step 5 says confirm stable, and Step 7 says load stable and alarms clear. Only synchronization has a timeout or failure action. Nothing covers failing to reach 500 rpm, an interrupted warm-up hold, failing to reach 2000 or 3600 rpm, or a vacuum step timeout.
why.2: Step 4 blocks holds and setpoint stops in 1600-1900 rpm. A hold request in the band is rejected and the ramp continues to 2000 rpm. A stall (rate below minimum) raises an alarm, and the operator must either continue accelerating or drop below 1600 rpm.
why.3: The coastdown text says only 'lube oil maintained' and 'Lube oil pumps run as required'. It does not say that P-11 must take over as the shaft pump decays, or that P-12 backs up P-11 during coastdown. The turning gear part is covered: the DCS engages M-15 at zero speed. Overall the oil backup during coastdown is too vague.
why.4: Section 1 assigns overspeed to the Woodward governor and the sequencing to the DCS. It specifies a hardwired trip loop independent of both the DCS and the governor. Section 3.2 adds an independent hardwired overspeed module and the mechanical bolt, so overspeed does not rely on the DCS.
why.5: Section 3.8 specifies latching with first-out recording. Reset requires the cause to be cleared, zero speed, and operator acknowledgement. Permissive #1 (trip latch reset) means a restart has to go back through the sequence permissives.
why.6: Missing values are consistently marked [TBD] and stated as not invented. This covers warm/hot start holds, ramp rates and voting arrangements. The output flags the 2oo2 one-failed-probe behavior, the narrow 110/111% overspeed margin, and the single PT-210 transmitter. It also lists these as open points.

why.1: DO-11 gives explicit output breakpoints (0–33.3% agitator 80→140 rpm, 33.3–66.7% air 0→10 slpm, 66.7–100% O2 0→5 slpm) with upstream stages held at max. DO-13 requires each stage to reach max before the next starts and to unload in reverse order. DO-12 sets the 80 rpm minimum.
why.2: PH-04 and DO-04 set disagreement thresholds (0.10 pH; 10% air sat; 60 s) that raise a deviation alarm, with control continuing on the average and optional operator deselection. PH-02/DO-02 define single-probe control with an alarm, and PH-03/DO-03 define the both-bad case.
why.3: BL-03 raises a pre-alarm at 36 L. BL-04 stops and inhibits P-520 at 40 L with a critical alarm, and BL-05 makes this non-bypassable. BL-02 allows a totalizer reset only at the start of Media Fill for a new batch.
why.4: Hold (PD-07) and Abort/Stop (PD-08 → PD-05) are covered, and CO2, base pump and O2 final states are given. However, the agitator (SIC-530) and air valve (FIC-511) are only 'released to Harvest phase control'; no final state is defined for them, including on Abort.
why.5: The output never states that CO2 sparging affects dissolved gas/DO or defines any interaction or limit between the pH and DO loops. OI-5 only raises as an open question whether CO2 counts toward total sparge rate.
why.6: AU-01/AU-02 require a system-enforced reason before a Production setpoint change is accepted, rejecting blank or cancelled entries. AU-03 records date/time, user, tag, old/new value, reason and batch ID. AU-04 blocks faceplate bypass, and AU-07 makes records secure and non-editable.

why.1: Section 4.3 and DO-05 to DO-08 set the takeover conditions: air opens above baseline only when SIC-530 is at 140 rpm, and O2 opens only when FCV-511 is at 10 slpm. They also set the hand-back as reverse unwinding (O2, then air, then agitation), give the limits (80-140 rpm, ≤10 slpm, ≤5 slpm), and require anti-windup and bumpless transfer. The hysteresis value is TBD, but the transition logic is defined.
why.2: The A/B disagreement threshold and delay are left as [TBD], so no threshold is defined. PH-02 treats deviation as making a probe unhealthy but never says which probe is excluded or what the controller uses when the two simply disagree. The single-probe fallback and the alarm are specified, but the core disagreement handling is not.
why.3: PH-13 gives a pre-limit warning (e.g. 35 L, value TBD). PH-14 stops and inhibits P-520 at ≥40 L with a high-priority alarm while the acid side continues. PH-12 states the WT-521-based totalizer resets at batch start only, not at phase change.
why.4: The Harvest transition is defined: loops out of service, valves closed, P-520 stopped, agitator handed to phase logic. However, the Hold and Abort output states are explicitly [TBD] in PHA-04, so the required behavior on Hold and Abort is not stated.
why.5: DO-11 only names 'Total gas flow interaction with the CO2 sparge (pH) and overlay/vent limits' as [TBD]. It does not state the interaction between the loops or define any limit, so it is a vague gesture.
why.6: SP-01 to SP-03 require the system to demand a reason before a Production setpoint change is accepted. The change must be made under a privileged role, and a change without a reason is not applied. The record (tag, old/new value, time, user ID, reason) is stored non-editably in the batch record/audit trail.

why.1: Section 5 states Feed (lb/day) = Q_filtered × Total Dose × 8.34, with Total Dose = Base Dose + Trim. Section 6 clamps trim authority to ±1.0 mg/L (adjustable, max ±2.0) and applies it to dose, not feed rate.
why.2: Section 6 handles the deadtime concretely. It estimates flow-dependent deadtime as τd = 6×(40/Q) and gain-schedules a slow PI with Ti = 2×τd and low Kc. It offers sample-and-hold trim as an alternative, plus freeze timers in multiples of τd.
why.3: Section 10 treats each separately. FIT-401: bad signal or rate-of-change triggers hold of the last good value, an alarm, and after 15 min an escalated alarm recommending MANUAL. AIT-402: out of range, fault contact, low sample flow or flatline freezes trim with an alarm, and trim later decays to pure flow pacing (Section 6).
why.4: Overfeed protection includes the dose high clamp (5.0 mg/L), the feed clamp at 2000 lb/day, and AIT-402 High (3.0) and High-High (3.5) alarms, with High-High forcing trim negative. For AIT-403 near the 0.2 mg/L minimum: a Low alarm at 0.5 raises the trim lower clamp to 0, Low-Low at 0.3 triggers an operator callout, and below 0.2 starts a critical alarm and compliance timer.
why.5: Section 8 lists failover criteria: fault contact, 30 s vacuum loss, positioner discrepancy, and supply depleted (both containers below Low-Low weight). Section 9 gives container switchover at a 200 lb low-weight alarm via the vacuum switchover valve, with a 'Container Switchover – Replace Empty' alarm. Operator follow-up is defined: replace the empty container, enter tare, and use the Container Change in Progress button.
why.6: Section 11 covers both levels. At 1 ppm: horn/strobe, HMI priority alarm and callout. At 3 ppm: hardwired closure of XV-421/422, scrubber start, PLC sets both feeder outputs to 0, and a critical alarm. The shutdown latches and needs AE-420 below 1 ppm plus a manual local reset; container valves are reopened manually after inspection.

why.1: Section 4 gives Q_cl = FIT-401 [MGD] × D_total [mg/L] × 8.34 with D_total = D_base + D_trim. Section 5 clamps the trim output to ±1.0 mg/L around D_base with anti-windup, and D_total is also clamped to 0.5–3.5 mg/L.
why.2: Section 5 specifies a slow, conservative PI (Kc≈0.3, Ti 15–20 min, no derivative, 1-min execution). It adds freeze conditions during flow changes and flow-scheduled tuning, with a Smith predictor as a fallback.
why.3: The Section 7 table covers each failure separately. FIT-401 bad: hold last good flow 5 min, then an operator-entered fixed flow, with alarms and trim frozen. AIT-402 bad: trim frozen and revert to Flow Pace Only, with an alarm.
why.4: Overfeed protection: AIT-402 High/High-High/4.0 mg/L alarms with trim forced low and feed reduced or stopped, plus the D_total and Q_cl clamps. The AIT-403 response is tiered at 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 mg/L: high-priority alarm and trim allowed upward, critical alarm, then a latched regulatory-violation alarm.
why.5: Section 6.1 gives scale-weight switchover thresholds (200 lb alarm, 100 lb switchover, 50 lb trip). Section 6.2 lists feeder changeover triggers (vacuum loss, positioner fault, both containers empty) and a sequence. Operator follow-up is defined: alarm, no automatic return, failback by operator selection, manual container changeout with valves confirmed closed.
why.6: Section 9: at 1 ppm, alarm with no shutdown. At 3 ppm, close XV-421/422, start the scrubber, trip both feeders and lock out feed. The trip latches and reset needs AE-420 below 1 ppm plus a manual local reset; valves are reopened by hand.

why.1: The output says each listed controller starts its pump from its own sensing line. It says the PLC 'monitors only', that PT-601 is not a start sensor, and that the PLC has no start/stop authority and no outputs to FP-1, FP-2 or the ATS.
why.2: The output states that NFPA 20 allows diesel engine automatic shutdown only on overspeed. Low oil pressure and high coolant temperature are alarms only, and the PLC has no trips of any kind. The Section 6 table reflects this.
why.3: The output rejects the PLC's 'pressure recovered' stop and recommends manual stop at the controller. Automatic shutdown is allowed only inside the listed controller, with 10/30 min minimum run timers and AHJ/insurer approval, stated explicitly.
why.4: The output keeps the 155/165, 145 and 135 psig setpoints and checks the gaps against Annex guidance. It notes the 10 psi margin guards against nuisance starts. It defines a PLC excessive jockey cycling alarm as an indication of system leakage.
why.5: The output gives a tagged PLC input list with descriptions, signal types and the PLC alarm/action (alarm priority, logging). It also states that PLC, power or network loss has no effect on the pumps. However, it does not define the operator response for each alarm; the action column only gives alarm priority or logging. Signal source is given generically rather than per point.
why.6: Section 1 has a corrections table giving the client's intent, the issue tied to NFPA 20 requirements, and the corrected intent. It includes plain-language rationale, such as the single point of failure and the design choice to run the engine to destruction.

why.1: Sections 1, 2 and 7 state that the listed controllers start the pumps from their own pressure sensing. They say the PLC is a monitoring and annunciation layer outside the start/stop path and issues no automatic start commands.
why.2: Section 2 marks the low lube oil and high coolant trips as 'Not permitted' and alarm-only. It says the only automatic engine shutdown allowed is overspeed, and repeats this in section 7.
why.3: It rejects the PLC 10-minute auto-stop. The default is manual stop at the controller. The controller's run-period timer is allowed only after an automatic start and only if the AHJ approves, and this is stated explicitly.
why.4: The staggered setpoints (155/165, 145, 135) are kept, with the stagger noted. However, excessive jockey pump cycling is never flagged as an alarm or leak indication; only 'JP-1 run and fail' is monitored.
why.5: The alarm list gives signal sources (hardwired dry contacts from each controller, plus process signals), and section 1 says PLC loss must not affect pump operation. No operator response is defined for any alarm.
why.6: Section 2 has a correction table that gives a plain-language reason for each change, tied to NFPA 20 and fire protection intent (single point of failure, run-to-failure). It closes by recommending a note to the client explaining the corrections.

why.1: Section 3.3/3.4 set measurable stage-up triggers: CHWST more than 1.5°F above setpoint, average %RLA above 90%, load above 90% of operating capacity, and flow above 1,700 gpm. Stage-down requires load below 70% of remaining capacity, CHWST within 0.5°F, and minimum run time elapsed. Section 1.6 sets stage-up (10 min), stage-down (15 min) and interstage (15 min) delays, plus minimum run (30 min) and minimum off (15 min, or anti-recycle if longer) times.
why.2: Section 5 sets the minimum flow setpoint as chillers running × 960 gpm × 1.10, with FCV-701 modulated from FIT-702. It covers meter location, backup flow from evaporator ΔP, and per-chiller low-flow protection at 1,000 gpm. For staging transitions, 3.5 requires a slow isolation valve stroke limited to the manufacturer's allowable flow-change rate and a demand limit on running chillers, and 3.6 keeps pumps and valves open during post-run.
why.3: Section 10.1 covers a chiller trip: critical alarm, lockout, and immediate stage-up of the next available chiller using the 3.5 procedure with delays bypassed. That procedure includes the condenser pump, CHWP and tower cell sequencing. It also releases demand limits and suspends reset. Section 3.3e also gives immediate stage-up on a trip.
why.4: Section 6.4 returns the setpoint to 42°F and suspends reset when any critical or surgery AHU valve is above 80%, discharge air temperature is above setpoint, supply dewpoint is high, OR RH is above 55%, OA dewpoint is high, and other conditions. Section 6.5 explains the humidity basis.
why.5: Section 10.4a states that chillers revert to local control and keep running at the local 42°F setpoint, with hardwired enables latched or failing to enabled. Pump and tower VFDs go to preset speeds, FCV-701 fails open, and controllers are on UPS with redundant controller architecture.
why.6: Section 1.5 rotates weekly on Monday at 10:00, with the unit having the fewest run hours becoming lead. Rotation never stops a running unit and takes effect at the next staging event. Manual lead fixing is allowed, and rotation can optionally be inhibited during OR occupied hours.

why.1: Section 4 sets stage-up thresholds (90% average load, CHWST +1.5°F at limit, calculated load 90%) with a 10 min delay, plus immediate staging at +3°F or on a trip. Stage-down thresholds are 75% and 85% projected load with a 15 min delay. Minimum run time is 20 min and minimum off time is 10 min.
why.2: 5.3 has FCV-701 hold FIT-702 at 960 gpm × chillers running plus margin. FIT-702 is a common loop meter, so this does not ensure each running chiller stays above 960 gpm. For staging, 4.3 only says the pump starts and the isolation valve opens slowly. It does not say how the bypass setpoint or valve is handled during the transition, such as raising the minimum flow target or pre-opening the bypass before a valve opens or closes.
why.3: 4.1 and 8.3 start the standby unit immediately on a chiller trip, with an alarm and staggered starts. The unit start sequence in 3.1 covers isolation valves, CWP, CHWP flow proving and tower enable before the chiller starts.
why.4: 7.2 disables reset and returns CHWST to 42°F under four conditions: any surgery suite AHU valve over 90% open, any critical zone temperature or humidity alarm, capacity below N+1, or a DPT-710 fault. Reset uses trim-and-respond with rate limits.
why.5: 8.5 states that on communication loss the chillers keep running on onboard controls. Pumps go to a fixed speed, FCV-701 holds position or fails open, and towers hold last speed or a fixed speed. The plant does not shut down.
why.6: 1.5 sets rotation on runtime (weekly, adjustable) and on lead failure. Nothing states that rotation must start the incoming unit and prove it before stopping the outgoing one, so rotation could drop running capacity.

why.1: Problem 4 flags 1200 in 4.3.2 versus 1400 in 4.3.7. The corrected 4.3.4 defines the target once as a configurable recipe parameter marked '[TBC — one value only]', and 4.3.7 refers only to 'the target'.
why.2: Problem 1 notes the trip at 9.0 barg would fire before the alarm at 9.5 barg. Corrected 4.3.5 requires the high-high to be above the high alarm and below the relief valve set pressure, with values marked TBC, and the engineer is asked for design and relief pressures.
why.3: Problem 2 says fail-open lets steam flow uncontrolled into a closed pressure vessel on air loss. Corrected 4.3.6 makes FV-812 and the shutoff valve fail-closed.
why.4: 'Check pressure is OK' becomes defined PT-811 alarm and trip logic. 'If possible' venting becomes a 'shall' requirement with a valve tag, defined control-basis options and alarm-and-hold behavior if the turpentine system is unavailable. Numeric values are TBC placeholders, not invented.
why.5: Problem 5 identifies automatic start in 4.3.2 versus operator request in 4.3.7. Corrected 4.3.7 consistently requires operator confirmation and blow permissives.
why.6: Adds TT-810 failure handling (alarm and freeze H-factor integration), HOLD on trip during cooking, a ramp deviation alarm and a TT-810 high alarm. It also states that H-factor integration behavior during trips must be defined. LT-805 failure is not addressed, but the expectation is satisfied by example.

why.1: Problem 3 flags the 1200 vs 1400 conflict and recommends a single recipe parameter. Corrected 4.3.3 states the target once as a recipe value marked 'to be confirmed', and it is listed in the open items.
why.2: Problem 1 flags that the 9.0 barg trip is below the 9.5 barg alarm. Corrected 4.3.5 requires y > x, keeps the trip below the relief valve set pressure, and asks for confirmation against the design basis.
why.3: Problem 2 says fail-open would drive uncontrolled steam and risk overpressure and overtemperature. Corrected 4.3.6 specifies that FV-812 shall fail closed on loss of air or signal.
why.4: Problem 4 calls out 'OK' and 'if possible' as vague. Corrected 4.3.4 replaces them with automatic pressure-controlled venting to the turpentine/NCG system via a tagged valve at a setpoint, stating venting shall not depend on operator action.
why.5: Problem 8 identifies the automatic-start vs operator-request inconsistency. Corrected 4.3.7 states blow initiation in one place with an explicit 'select one' choice, listed as an open item.
why.6: Problem 7 and corrected 4.3.3 add a temperature tolerance band, an alarm on deviation, and an explicit decision point on whether H-factor accumulation holds or continues. Problem 5 also asks for LT-805 failure behavior. Weakness: no explicit TT-810 or LT-805 signal-failure handling appears in the corrected text.

why.1: The output flags the contradiction ('It can't be both'). It never explicitly picks one strategy, such as MOV reset with clamps or a truly fixed setpoint. It only implies MOV by listing reset parameters.
why.2: Item B says closing the valve risks septic conditions and solids settling. It proposes an alarm plus an operator-adjustable fallback airflow or position no lower than the minimum mixing airflow.
why.3: Item A converts 7.5 psig to about 208 inH2O and notes that 160/165 inH2O is about 5.8–6.0 psig, so the staging band doesn't match the setpoint. It recommends using one unit throughout.
why.4: Missing Content flags surge protection (minimum flow/blow-off or IGV minimum) as a significant omission. Item B notes that valve closure pushes the blowers toward surge.
why.5: Item C flags stacked inrush current and the personnel hazard. It requires staggered restarts with adjustable delays and an operator-selectable enable/disable.
why.6: The vibration trip gap is fully flagged (tag, setpoints, delay, latched reset). However, the output only asks for a tag for the discharge valve switch. It never questions whether a discharge-valve-open permissive suits centrifugal blower starting practice.

why.1: Critical issue 1 says item 2 describes the setpoint as both fixed at 7.5 psig and reset by MOV logic. It says to pick one, and recommends a floating setpoint with min/max limits, reset rate and deadband.
why.2: Critical issue 4 says closing the valve will starve the biology and can cause septicity. It proposes holding the last good position or going to a fixed preset or minimum mixing position, and it calls for an alarm on the loss.
why.3: Critical issue 2 converts 7.5 psig to about 208 inH2O and 160/165 inH2O to about 5.8/6.0 psig. It explains that the setpoint and staging thresholds don't agree, so blowers would keep staging off.
why.4: The output flags missing blow-off/recycle, surge protection and minimum airflow for centrifugal machines. It never ties surge risk to the MOV logic lowering pressure or to valve closure reducing flow. Its minimum-position point is about mixing, not blower surge.
why.5: Critical issue 5 flags the simultaneous auto-restart as unsafe because of inrush and possible generator or utility trip. It proposes a restart delay with a staggered sequence and permissives.
why.6: The vibration trip gaps (tags, alarm/trip setpoints, delay, startup bypass, manual reset) are covered. For item 4, the output only notes the missing discharge valve limit switch tag. It never questions whether a 'discharge valve open' permissive fits typical centrifugal blower starting practice or needs confirming.

why.1: D5 flags the PIC-510/PV-512 tag mismatch and asks for loop numbers aligned with the P&ID. The corrected section defines each controller explicitly: PIC-501 on PT-501 for compressors, PIC-512 on PT-512 for flare. It treats the loops as two distinct controllers rather than naming PIC-501 vs PIC-510 as one controller, but it does resolve the inconsistency into defined tags and functions.
why.2: D1 says tripping the compressors on high-high removes the main relief path and drives the tank toward its PSVs. The corrected 6.2.4 keeps the compressors running and forces PV-512 fully open. The corrected 6.2.5 trips the compressors on PALL (low-low).
why.3: D3 calls low pressure/vacuum a credible hazard and lists its causes. The corrected section adds PAL at 60 mbarg, a low-pressure override, makeup gas, and a PALL SIF at 30 mbarg that trips K-501A/B, all above the -5 mbarg vacuum relief.
why.4: D2 and corrected 6.2.6 cover all required elements: no HMI bypass, key/permit authorization, logging, a time limit with expiry alarm, a persistent HMI alarm, compensating measures per the SRS, and sensor-level degradation only.
why.5: D11 says the vendor anti-surge reference lacks an interface definition and covers its interaction with PIC-501, recycle cooling and trip/permissive signals. Corrected 6.2.8 requires an interface schedule with capacity demand, running/trip status, permissives and SIS trip inputs, and assigns recycle/anti-surge to the vendor package.
why.6: D7 says the setpoint hierarchy cannot be verified and that margins for valve stroke time, transmitter accuracy and accumulation are missing. D9 flags the missing PAH/PAL between control and trips. The corrected section adds a full hierarchy table from PSV down to VRV. It does not quantify the specific 220/250/290 gaps, but it does address coherence and margins.

why.1: The output never flags the PIC-501 vs PIC-510 inconsistency as a defect or asks for one defined tag/function. It treats them as two intentional, separate controllers and only asks for independent transmitters (defect 7). Defect 13 flags a different mismatch (PIC-510 vs PV-512).
why.2: Defect 1 says tripping the compressors on PAHH removes the main vapour-removal mitigation when it is most needed. The corrected section keeps the compressors running on PAHH and trips them on PALL in 6.2.5.
why.3: Defect 3 calls vacuum a credible failure mode and notes that air ingress via the vacuum relief valve is hazardous. The corrected 6.2.5 adds PAL at 70 mbarg (reduce capacity) and PALL at 40 mbarg (trip compressors), both well above the -5 mbarg vacuum relief point.
why.4: Defect 2 and corrected 6.2.4 prohibit HMI bypass. They require a key-switch, permit-to-work/MoC, an alarm, a time limit and documented compensating measures.
why.5: Defect 12 says the one-line vendor reference is not a functional requirement and that the interface to tank pressure control is missing. Corrected 6.2.7 requires the anti-surge/recycle interaction with PIC-501 to be specified and a DCS/SIS interface list to be supplied for review. Recycle valve ownership is not explicitly named.
why.6: Defect 8 reviews the ladder (120/220/250/290), notes the narrow gaps between flare, PAHH and PSV, and notes that design pressure and accumulation are not stated. The corrected section adds PAH at 180 and a low-side ladder.

why.1: Issue 1 says the E-stop appears only as a standard PLC input. It requires a hardwired safety relay or safety PLC and notes that no stop category or reset behavior is defined. The revision then defines Stop Category 0/1 and a reset sequence.
why.2: Issue 2 says automatic restart on door close is not permitted. It requires a deliberate reset plus start from outside the guarded area, and the revision repeats this.
why.3: Issue 3 maps external blocked/starved conditions to Suspended and internal conditions or operator Hold to Held. It states that Stop goes Stopping → Stopped, and the revised state table matches.
why.4: Issue 5 notes that 'PE-320 blocked' triggers on every passing product and needs a continuous-blocked time. The revision sets T_jam to 2× normal product transit time at current speed.
why.5: Starvation goes to Suspended and auto-resumes once PE-310 is continuously blocked for 3 s, an accumulation threshold. It is explicitly classed as not a fault, unlike the jam, which requires Reset and Start.
why.6: Issue 7 calls the single number 'not a spec' and lists the missing setpoint source, conveyor speed tracking and accel/decel. The revision adds an access-protected setpoint source, ramps and conveyor speed tracking.

why.1: The output says the E-stop on standard input I:3/0 depends on PLC logic and is single-channel. It requires a hardwired, dual-channel, monitored safety relay or safety PLC. It requires choosing a stop category (0 or 1) per drive and a latching, deliberate manual reset.
why.2: The output calls auto-resume after door closing a hazard, citing unexpected restart and a person possibly inside. It requires that the machine stay stopped until a manual Reset and a deliberate Start, with a start-up warning horn.
why.3: The output states that downstream full and upstream starved map to Suspended as external conditions. It states that operator Stop goes to Stopping → Stopped and that Held is for internal or operator-initiated holds. The revised state model reflects all of this.
why.4: The output flags that 'PE-320 blocked' alone will false-trip and adds a continuous blocked-time delay ([x s, adjustable]). However, it never ties the threshold to machine or conveyor speed, which the expectation requires.
why.5: Starvation goes to Suspended with a warning, not a fault. It auto-resumes once bottles are detected for [x s], which is an accumulation/confirmation threshold. This is contrasted with jam/fault handling, which requires operator clearance and Reset.
why.6: The output flags 30 cases/min as underspecified: rated vs setpoint, adjustable range, accel/decel ramp rates, conveyor speeds derived from the setpoint, and whether infeed throughput matches. It also places setpoint adjustment on the HMI. It does not specify access level, but the key gaps (fixed value, ramps, upstream/downstream interaction) are covered.

why.1: C4 says Step 2 goes straight from crank to fuel. It adds a timed starter-crank purge of the combustor and exhaust before light-off, vendor-specified, often 3 or more exhaust volume changes.
why.2: M1 flags missing step timeouts and start abort ('fail to achieve within X s, abort to safe state'), a trial-for-ignition timer and maximum light-off attempts. M3 adds 'Flame proven within T s, otherwise abort and purge' and a separate self-sustaining-speed milestone, so purge before retry is covered.
why.3: C1 states blowdown valves must fail open and block valves fail closed, explains why fail-closed is dangerous, and gives corrected wording.
why.4: C2 requires removing auto-restart and latching the ESD. Reset needs cleared initiators, a deliberate manual reset and investigation per site procedure, and each restart needs an operator Start command.
why.5: M7 rejects 'see vendor data' as neither implementable nor testable. It requires stated alarm and trip setpoints with units, voting between the probes (2oo2/1oo2), trip delay and fault handling.
why.6: M4 says loading at idle is usually wrong, that step closure of the recycle valve at low speed invites surge, and that the anti-surge controller must ramp it closed. C3 flags ESD in the same PLC as a common-cause failure and recommends an independent SIL-rated logic solver per IEC 61511.

why.1: Item 4 says Step 3 goes from cranking straight to fuel and ignition. It requires a crank/purge of the turbine and exhaust for a specified number of volume changes or time before fuel is admitted.
why.2: Item 4 lists ignition and flame-proving timeouts, a failure-to-light response (fuel off, abort, re-purge, retry limit, lockout), and starter cutout and start-failure timers. Item 7 adds a timeout and abort for pressure equalization.
why.3: Item 2 flags fail-closed blowdown as defeating ESD on utility loss. It never says the valves should fail open, and it allows fail-closed to stay with a risk assessment or other means. The correction is hedged, not stated.
why.4: Item 1 says auto-restart should be removed. It requires a manual ESD reset, a field walkdown, and a deliberate operator Start through permissives.
why.5: Item 10 says 'see vendor data' should be replaced with actual setpoints, units and time delays. It also flags missing 1oo2/2oo2 voting for VT-2201/2202 and bad-sensor behavior.
why.6: Item 8 calls recycle closure at idle potentially unsafe and requires a ramped closure, active anti-surge control and a defined response to surge. Item 5 questions the shared PLC and calls for an independent SIL-rated or hardwired safety layer.

why.1: Issue 1 gives a timeline showing 3 s + crank + 5 s stabilization + sync + transfer comes to about 17–27 s, which exceeds 10 s. It names waiting for both generators to parallel as the main cause. The fix is to transfer ATS-L and ATS-C as soon as the first generator closes to the dead bus.
why.2: Issue 3 rejects simultaneous transfer. The revised sequence transfers ATS-L and ATS-C first when the first generator is on the bus, then ATS-E on a delay after the second generator synchronizes and capacity is confirmed. Life safety and critical share the first tier, with equipment last.
why.3: Issue 6 replaces 'as required' with defined priorities: ATS-L and ATS-C are never shed, and ATS-E loads are ranked into shed blocks. Triggers are generator kW at about 90–100%, under-frequency and generator failure, each with time delays. Restoration adds loads back automatically and in sequence, by priority, as capacity returns.
why.4: Issue 5 and step 7 add an adjustable retransfer delay of about 30 min after the utility proves stable, bypassed if the emergency source fails. Step 8 adds an unloaded cool-down of at least 5 min before the generators stop.
why.5: Issue 4 says low coolant temperature and low fuel should be alarms only, citing NFPA 110 Table 5.6.5.2 for Level 1. It limits shutdowns to overspeed, low oil pressure, high coolant temperature and overcrank, and explains why each change matters.
why.6: The output criticizes the length of the 3 s delay and proposes about 1 s. It never points out that 3.1 says 'starts both generators immediately' while 3.2 adds a 3 s confirmation delay, so it does not flag or explicitly resolve that inconsistency.

why.1: Issue 1 adds up 3 s + 6-10 s start + 5 s stabilization + sync and concludes it exceeds 10 s. Issue 2 flags that nothing transfers until both units are online. The restructure transfers ATS-L and ATS-C as soon as the first generator closes to the dead bus, all within 10 s.
why.2: Issue 3 rejects simultaneous transfer. The restructure transfers life safety and critical immediately, then ATS-E after a delay, in steps and only with kW headroom. This sets the priority, though L and C transfer together rather than strictly one after the other.
why.3: The output says 3.3 lacks a priority, a kW threshold and restore rules, and it requires that life safety and critical are never shed. It never supplies an actual shed priority list or a defined order for adding load back. It only says 'shed it in a defined priority order' and mentions kW-permissive steps, so it points at the need rather than meeting it.
why.4: Issue 6 specifies a retransfer delay of several minutes to 30 min with stability confirmation, and an unloaded cooldown of about 5 min before stopping. It also covers retransfer to the generators if utility fails again during cooldown.
why.5: It correctly flags low coolant temperature and low fuel as alarm-only and cites NFPA 110. However, it also says high coolant temperature should not be a shutdown, which contradicts NFPA 110's permitted or required Level 1 shutdowns. It omits low oil pressure and keeps only overspeed and overcrank. The retained shutdown list and its basis are therefore inaccurate.
why.6: Issue 7 explicitly notes that 3.1 says 'start immediately' while 3.2 starts after the 3 s delay. It resolves this by starting on the first loss signal and treating the delay only as a qualifier, and the restructure has both generators start on utility failure.

why.1: Section 2 Causes covers the tag, the condition with direction (PV < SP / PV > SP), voting (1oo1/2oo3), a Delay ID and a Hysteresis/Reset ID. Section 4 Effects gives the action on trip and the fail-safe position (FC/FO/FL) for each final element.
why.2: There is a Bad-quality action column (treat as tripped / alarm only / hold last) covering open circuit, out of range and comms loss. Section 6 covers reset conditions, reset location and authority, and auto versus operator release. Section 3 covers latched versus non-latching.
why.3: Section 7 covers whether bypass is allowed, the method and authority, indication and alarm, and maximum duration with auto-removal. The header has a 'Related SIS function (not documented here)' field pointing to the SIF ID in the SRS, and the title scopes the sheet to BPCS.
why.4: Sheets hold only Setpoint IDs that point to a single Trip & Alarm Setpoint Register. The rules prevent drift: the register is the only source, other documents use the ID only, the DCS export is compared automatically to the register at FAT, test records note the value applied and the register revision, and changes go through MOC on the register only.
why.5: Section 10 is a test matrix with initial conditions, action, expected result, pass/fail, value applied and register revision, and a § cross-reference. A list of minimum test cases is included, and the example shows 12 executable test cases.
why.6: Most of the example is sound and consistent with the template: XV-1106 closes fail-closed, pilots are explicitly unaffected, the trip is latched, reset excludes PT-1105 for a stated reason, and a start-up inhibit is defined. However, neither the relight sequence nor the reset section requires a purge before relight or gives a reason why none is needed. It only says the valve may be opened 'if the BMS permissives are healthy'. Under strict reading that is a vague gesture, so this required element is missing.

why.1: Section 3 lists the input tag(s) and has a Voting column. Section 4.1 states the trip condition as a Boolean with direction (e.g. PV < SP). Section 4.2 covers on-delay, off-delay and hysteresis. Section 6 gives the action on each output and the final element fail position and output state.
why.2: Section 3 has a column for quality handling (bad, open-circuit, out of range), and 4.7 covers fault behavior. Section 4.4 covers whether the trip is latched, the reset permissives, who resets and from where.
why.3: Section 4.5 covers whether bypass is allowed, the authority, method, maximum duration, alarm on bypass and auto-restore. Section 2 is an SIS boundary check confirming the function is not an SIF, naming any related SIS function and stating the basis for BPCS classification.
why.4: Section 5 is the only place setpoint values appear. All other sections refer to setpoint IDs, each mapped to a single DCS parameter. The rules explain that alarm DB, HMI and FAT read the value rather than retype it, and the practical suggestions generate both the sheet and the DCS import from one controlled database. This explicitly addresses drift.
why.5: Section 11 provides FAT step columns: pre-condition, action (values as formulas from the register), expected result, section verified, and pass/fail sign-off. These are directly usable as test steps.
why.6: The example correctly closes XV-1106 on low pressure, with a latched trip, manual reset and fail-closed valve. However, it never states pilot handling, and it does not require a purge before relight or give a reason for omitting one. It only says 'follow restart procedure', even though it names relight into a hot firebox as a hazard. FAT step 1 also has an inconsistent hold-time formulation.

why.1: Layer A type narratives define modes (Auto/Manual/OOS), states and transitions (Stopped→Starting→Running→Stopping→Stopped, Faulted from any state) and command sources once each for EM-PMP and EM-VLV. Governing rule 1 says instances may reference clause IDs but never restate them.
why.2: PMP-5 defines fail to start and fail to stop on P_FbTime (5 s), unexpected stop with debounce, and drive/overload fault, each with an action. PMP-6.1.4 covers VFD comm loss. VLV-5 covers travel timeout, position loss and both-switches discrepancy. PMP-7 defines reset rules.
why.3: PMP-2.4 states that a mode change does not change the output state (bumpless), with an example. PMP-2.5 covers a phase acquiring a non-Auto EM. PMP-8 defines power-up and PLC restart behaviour (Auto, Stopped, latches cleared except feature trips).
why.4: Layer B Instance Register lists tag, type/version, features, I/O, parameter overrides only, interlock IDs and exceptions. P-4021 has a register entry, an override-only parameter table, an interlock extract and an exception record. Valves are shown as table rows.
why.5: P-4021 specifies P_DrySP 0.8 bar(g), P_DryArmT 15 s after start, P_DryT 5 s, and bad-quality action Trip, with the trip action referenced to PMP-6.2. The speed source is the CIP-40 supply phase flow controller output. Section 5.4 explicitly avoids restating the generic behaviour.
why.6: Type narratives are versioned with the library, and Register rows name a library version. Exceptions require Library Change Requests tracked to zero. A library upgrade triggers a documentation impact review. The Register is the single source of truth, generating or diffed against the PLC data.

why.1: Layer A defines a class narrative written once per class: EM-PUMP-FIXED, EM-PUMP-VFD and EM-VALVE-ONOFF. Its sections cover modes (Auto, Manual, Out of Service, Simulation), commands, and a state table (Stopped, Starting, Running, Stopping, Faulted) with transitions. Instance sheets reference the class by ID and version and 'never restate class behavior'. The class content is a skeleton, but the structure of define-once and reference is clearly established.
why.2: Faults appear only as headings. There is 'Feedback supervision… with default timeouts as class parameters' and a placeholder 'Standard faults and alarms' table. No fail-to-start/stop conditions, valve fail-to-open/close or position discrepancy logic, VFD fault actions, timing values or reset types are actually defined. Valve travel timeouts are only mentioned as an instance override topic.
why.3: Only headings are given: 'what happens on mode change' and 'Power loss and restart behavior'. Manual-to-auto transfer behavior, bumpless output handling and restart-after-power-restoration behavior are never specified.
why.4: The instance sheet template lists I/O tags, permissives, interlocks and parameter overrides (only non-default values). It also has an explicit Deviations table with ID, justification and approval. The P-4021 example fills these in.
why.5: P-4021 dry-run protection on PT-4022 is documented: start threshold 40 kPa, trip threshold 20 kPa, 5 s trip delay, and a 10 s start-up mask. The action is to stop the pump and raise the Dry-Run Trip alarm, with manual reset. The speed source is stated: the setpoint comes from the active CIP step via the sequence. Section 5 confirms that generic pump behavior is not restated.
why.6: Rule 6 requires that a class change bumps the version and lists affected instances, and that instances are deliberately re-pinned. Instances pin a class version, and recurring deviations trigger a class update. The FAT check compares the PLC against the document to catch drift.

why.1: It turns the vague notes into testable criteria with units: ramp 30–50 °C/h, coal changeover permissive back-end ≥600 °C, feed start at back-end 900–1000 °C with ≈40 % of design feed. Note-derived values are shown in italics with the operator's wording, and anything needing confirmation is marked [TBC].
why.2: The rotation schedule table is entirely [TBC]; '¼ or ⅓' turns appear only as examples. The feed ramp keeps 'a few hours' and its profile is [TBC]. Other undefined values (trip setpoints, firing rates, intervals) are flagged [TBC] rather than invented.
why.3: It is automatic logic, not a watch item: alarm level, trip level, automatic ESP HV trip on all fields, analyzer-fault fail-safe, no bypass, and reset only after CO is below the reset level for [TBC] min plus an operator reset. However, no trip delay or filter time is defined for the trip itself; the only time element is on reset. Judged strictly, the required delay element is missing.
why.4: Section 6.4 and permissive P4 make an emergency power source (genset/UPS) for the aux drive a design requirement. The trigger is loss of main power with a hot kiln. Actions are fuel trip, transfer of the aux drive to emergency power, and a cool-down rotation schedule. A manual turning backup and periodic testing are also required.
why.5: Section 5 tables which functions are automatic and which need operator confirmation or are semi-automatic. Section 6.1 makes the ID fan 60 % a hard low limit on the controller output while flame is proven, with a fuel trip on violation.
why.6: Section 8 lists 13 specific interview questions for the operator. [TBC] items throughout point to the process engineer, vendors and the refractory supplier, and gaps are stated explicitly rather than hidden.

why.1: The output turns the vague items into values with units: heat-up limit 30–50 °C/h at the back end, coal changeover at about 600 °C back-end, and feed start at about 40% once the tower is hot and back-end is 900–1000 °C. It states that values not in the notes are marked [CONFIRM], and it applies that marking consistently.
why.2: The aux-drive turn schedule, main-drive transition temperature, feed ramp rate and step size, and CO setpoints are all left as [CONFIRM]. The notes give only a trend for these, and no precise values were invented.
why.3: Interlock I-2 makes CO rising at the inlet analyzer an automatic trip that de-energizes the ESP. It names the CO trip threshold, alarm level, time delay and reset conditions as parameters to define, and proposes a two-stage alarm and trip. Values are flagged rather than invented.
why.4: Section 8 does make a backup source for the aux drive a requirement (emergency generator or UPS), with auto-start on loss of main drive. However, it defines no operator actions; it says 'no operator action required'. It also leaves the rotation pattern during the outage as [CONFIRM], and does not address securing firing or verifying rotation on power loss.
why.5: The ID fan below 60% while firing is an interlock that prevents or trips firing, so it is an enforced limit, with only the trip type left to confirm. The output separates automatic actions (ESP trip, aux auto-start, rate-limited ramp with a logged operator override) from operator responses (shell hot-spot alarm with operator action).
why.6: Section 9 lists nine open items for confirmation, and Section 10 recommends interviewing the operator about judgment-based rules before they retire.

why.1: FR-03 to FR-08 describe the behaviour functionally with units: lead runs in Auto without fault, lag starts after PT101 < 18.5 bar for 8 s or immediately on lead fault, lag stops when PT101 > 21.0 bar (hysteresis 18.5/21.0 bar). These are grouped by function rather than paraphrased line by line.
why.2: Section 4.x.5 states that LagLatched is never reset and stays TRUE permanently after the first lag start. Section 4.x.7 explains the consequence: after rotation the outgoing pump stops only above 21.0 bar, so both pumps can keep running. OI-3 requires a decision and recommends defining a reset for LagLatched.
why.3: OI-1 (Critical, safety) explicitly says that stopping feed pumps on low drum level is the opposite of correct practice, since low drum level calls for more feed and a burner trip. It suggests LT100 may really be suction-side (feedwater tank/deaerator) level, and requires field verification before any design work.
why.4: OI-5 identifies Maint_B7 forcing LT100_Lo FALSE as an undocumented maintenance bypass with no timeout, alarm or permit. It requires cross-referencing, and re-implementation only under a formal bypass procedure with access control, alarm, time limit and logging.
why.5: Section 4.x.7 and OI-4 note the missing edge detection: LeadSel toggles every scan for the full minute, so the outcome is random. They also note there is no changeover sequence and both pumps may keep running afterwards. The intended behaviour is defined: one-shot trigger, start new lead, prove running/pressure, then stop old lead, and rotate only if the standby pump is healthy.
why.6: The as-found behaviours are labelled separately from a dedicated Open Items table (OI-1 to OI-9). The status banner says not to implement verbatim. Section 4.x.9 requires each item to be closed as 'replicate as found' or 'corrected' in a separate approved target revision.

why.1: FR-2 through FR-6 describe the behaviour functionally with units: lead runs in auto when not faulted, lag starts after PT101 is below 18.5 bar for 8 s or on lead fault, and lag stops above 21.0 bar. The output also explains hysteresis and scan-order priority instead of paraphrasing line by line.
why.2: Issue 4 states that LagLatched is never cleared, so after the first lag start the FR-5 stop is always permitted. It asks for the intended reset condition to be defined, with examples.
why.3: FR-6 carries the trip of both pumps on LT100 < 15% into the spec. It only questions the missing latch, reset or hysteresis (Issue 5). It never challenges that stopping feed pumps on low drum level is wrong for a boiler, and never asks whether LT100 actually measures a deaerator or suction tank.
why.4: FR-7 notes that Maint_B7 forces LT100_Lo FALSE and marks its purpose as unknown. However, it explicitly says the flag does not bypass FR-6 and treats it as a curiosity. It does not frame it as a hidden low-level bypass needing a decision, authorization and indication.
why.5: Issue 1 identifies that the toggle runs on every scan during the 06:00 minute and proposes a one-shot. Issue 3 covers running pumps at changeover, where both pumps end up running, and asks for the intended changeover behaviour to be defined.
why.6: Inferred items are tagged [Confirm] inline. Section 4 lists the issues to resolve separately, and Section 5 recommends verification against the live PLC and operating procedures.
